ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of multiples to find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of two or more numbers. Encourage a systematic approach when listing multiples, and discuss with students that, while multiples are infinite, they only need to list enough to identify a common one. Prompt them to highlight any common multiples before identifying the lowest common multiple. Once confident, students can progress to word problems and examples involving more than two numbers. Discuss the difference between the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple, helping students to understand when each one is used. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple. • Students may assume that the product of the two numbers is the lowest common multiple, for example that 36 is the lowest common multiple of 3 and 12 • Students may incorrectly list the multiples of two numbers. ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students build on previous learning to use Venn diagrams to find the highest common factor (HCF) and lowest common multiple (LCM). Ensure that students are confident in expressing numbers as a product of their prime factors before introducing this method. Model how to represent the prime factors of two numbers in a Venn diagram, emphasising that the intersection shows the shared prime factors. Explain that multiplying the numbers in the intersection gives the highest common factor, while multiplying all the numbers in the Venn diagram gives the lowest common multiple. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse which factors are multiplied to calculate the highest common factor or the lowest common multiple. • Students may duplicate prime factors in the Venn diagrams when they appear in both numbers. • Students may not understand that if there are no common prime factors in the intersection, then the highest common factor is 1 Year 7 | Summer term | Block 2 – Properties of numbers | Step 10 Mathematical talk • Express as a product of its prime factors. • Where in the Venn diagram do you write the common prime factors? • How do you calculate the highest common factor from a Venn diagram? • How do you calculate the lowest common multiple from a Venn diagram? • Explain why multiplying all the prime factors in the Venn diagram gives the lowest common multiple. • If two numbers have no common prime factors, what does the intersection of the Venn diagram contain? What does this tell you about their highest common factor? • What is the highest common factor when there are no common prime factors in the intersection of the Venn diagram? ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students develop flexibility in representing numbers by expressing them as a product of factors to simplify calculations. Encourage students to rewrite numbers in ways that make mental or written methods more efficient. For example, in the calculation 16 × 50, students could express 16 as 4 × 4 and 50 as 25 × 2, recognising that 4 × 25 = 100 and so simplifying the calculation to 100 × 4 × 2. Discuss the commutative property of multiplication, showing how reordering factors can make calculations easier. The focus is not on prime factorisation but on selecting factor groupings that simplify the process, helping students to develop efficient strategies for working without a calculator. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may write a value as a product of its prime factors, without considering how other representations may be more efficient. • Students may attempt to calculate the products in the order they are given, rather than looking for useful factor pairs that simplify the calculation, such as numbers that multiply to make 10 or 100 Year 7 | Summer term | Block 2 – Properties of numbers | Step 11 Mathematical talk • What are some useful factors of a number to identify? • Why is it useful to identify pairs of factors that multiply to give 10 or 100? • Write as a product of its factors. • Is writing a value as a product of its prime factors always the most efficient method? Explain how you know. • How many different ways can you express as a product of its factors? • Which product of factors is the most efficient for the calculation? Explain how you know. • Explain why multiplying the factors in any order still gives the same answer. E National Curriculum links • Use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors (or divisors), multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor, lowest common multiple, prime factorisation, including using product notation and the unique factorisation property

small_step_name: Add and subtract simple algebraic fractions (E)
ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students further develop their understanding of fractions within the context of algebra. Start by comparing the addition of fractional expressions to the addition of fractions in numerical form, keeping examples simple at this introductory stage, rather than using complex multi-term expressions. Provide practice with algebraic fractions that include variables in both numerators and denominators. If necessary, revisit the process of adding and subtracting fractions with different denominators before extending to algebraic cases. Where appropriate, challenge students with equations equal to a whole involving algebraic fractions, for example 3 x + 2 x = 1 Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not make the denominators equal before adding or subtracting the fractions. • Students may struggle to identify common denominators when the denominators are algebraic. • Students may incorrectly convert an expression into a fraction before adding or subtracting, for example x + 3x 4 = x x + 3x 4 Year 7 | Summer term | Block 3 – Add and subtract fractions | Step 9 National Curriculum links • Use the four operations, including formal written methods, applied to integers, decimals, proper and improper fractions, and mixed numbers, all both positive and negative • Use and interpret algebraic notation, including: ab in place of a × b; 3y in place of y + y + y and 3 × y; a2 in place of a × a, a3 in place of a × a × a; a2b in place of a × a × b; a b in place of a ÷ b; coefficients written as fractions rather than as decimals; brackets Mathematical talk • What is meant by “like terms”? • What is the same and what is different about 1 2 + 1 2 and a 2 + a 2 ? • How can you rewrite 3 x + 1 2x with equivalent denominators? • What is the same and what is different about x 4 and 1 4 x? • What does “in terms of m” mean? • Can the fraction be simplified? ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students apply their knowledge of adding and subtracting algebraic fractions within algebraic contexts, including substitution and solving equations. Start by focusing on substituting values into a range of algebraic fractional expressions. It may be helpful to revisit substitution in expressions without fractions before extending to those that include them. Similarly, when solving equations, recap methods for one- and two-step equations before introducing fractional terms, to support understanding. Where appropriate, provide additional challenge by including fractions greater than 1 in substitution problems or equations. small_step_name: Draw and measure lines and angles
ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop the practical skills of drawing and measuring line segments and angles accurately, building on understanding from Key Stage 2 Recap the correct use of a ruler for drawing and measuring line segments before introducing the protractor as the tool for measuring and drawing angles. Ensure that students know how to align the baseline and select the correct scale, modelling these skills clearly. Emphasise that an angle is a measure of turn. Provide questions where students both draw given angles and measure angles already drawn. Encourage them to estimate before measuring in order to develop a sense of size. Everyday contexts, such as design or navigation, help to show why accuracy matters. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misalign the protractor baseline with the line segment, leading to inaccurate measurements. • The term “line segment” may be unfamiliar and students may not realise that a line is infinite in length. • Students may read from the wrong scale on the protractor, for example 140° instead of 40°. • Students may misalign the ruler by not positioning the beginning of a line segment at zero. What strategies can you use to make sure that you are using the correct protractor scale? • Is the angle acute, right, obtuse or reflex? Explain how you know without measuring. • How would you use a protractor to measure an angle greater than 180°? ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students apply known angle facts to calculate unknown angles in a variety of contexts. At this stage, students should be confident in using all the angle facts covered so far in this block. The focus of this step is on identifying which fact to apply and justifying solutions using accurate mathematical vocabulary and notation. Encourage students to explain their thinking clearly and to check whether their answers are sensible. Model how to set up and solve equations based on different angle facts. More challenging questions may combine several angle facts, requiring a step-by- step approach to reach the solution. Calculators can be used to ensure that the focus remains on the application of the angle facts, rather than the arithmetic. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse which fact or facts apply to a situation. • Students may forget that vertically opposite angles are equal and instead assume that they sum to 180° or 360°. • Students may try to measure rather than calculate angles. • Students may not show clear reasoning or may use incorrect or incomplete justification when explaining their answers. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 9 Mathematical talk • What do you know? What can you find out? • What information can you add to the diagram? • How do you decide which angle fact to use and apply? • Is it possible to apply more than one angle fact in this problem? • Which angle facts do you know? • Which angle facts do you think you will need to apply to this problem? • How do you know whether to use 180° or 360° in a calculation? • How can you check that your answer is sensible once you have calculated an unknown angle? ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate and extend their Key Stage 2 understanding of parallel and perpendicular lines. Remind students that parallel lines are always the same distance apart and never meet, no matter how far they are extended. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle (90°), which can be shown using a square corner or set square. Use clear diagrams and practical examples, such as train tracks for parallel lines or the corner of a book for perpendicular lines. Encourage students to spot these relationships in shapes, coordinate grids and the classroom environment. Emphasise accurate vocabulary, such as “intersect” and “right angle”, and correct notation, including arrows for parallel lines and squares for right angles. Students should practise drawing parallel and perpendicular lines using a ruler and protractor or set square. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may assume that all lines that do not meet are parallel, overlooking the fact that parallel lines must also be equidistant. • Students may assume that lines need to be the same length to be parallel. • Students may confuse perpendicular lines with any intersecting lines. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 10 Mathematical talk • How can you tell that two lines are parallel? • What does it mean for two lines to be the same distance apart? • Can parallel lines ever meet? Explain your answer. • What makes a pair of lines perpendicular? • How can you check that two lines are perpendicular? • What is the same and what is different about parallel lines and perpendicular lines? • Where might you see parallel/perpendicular lines in everyday life? • If line AB is perpendicular to CD, and EF is parallel to AB, what is the relationship between EF and CD? National Curriculum links • Describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations: points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines, right angles, regular polygons, and other polygons that are reflectively and rotationally symmetric

small_step_name: Investigate angles in parallel lines  E
ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students explore angles formed when a transversal crosses parallel lines. The focus of this step is on careful measurement and observation of angles in parallel lines. Students investigate patterns and compare different angle positions. Encourage them to use known angle facts, such as angles on a straight line or around a point, to justify their ideas, where possible. Provide opportunities for students to test their conjectures with further examples to build confidence. This investigative approach develops curiosity and provides a secure foundation for introducing formal parallel line angle facts in later steps. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that all angles formed by a transversal and parallel lines are equal. • Students may believe that parallel lines must always be horizontal. • Students may not understand that there can be more than two parallel lines in a set. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 11 Mathematical talk • How can you identify parallel lines? • Do parallel lines always have to be drawn horizontally? Explain your answer. • How many angles are created when a transversal intersects a pair of parallel lines? • What do you notice about the sizes of the angles formed between a transversal and parallel lines? Is there a pattern? • Are there any other pairs of equal angles? Explain how you know. • If you know the size of one angle, how can you use angles on a straight line, vertically opposite angles and angles around a point to work out other angles? ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students are introduced to the sum of the interior angles in a polygon. Start with triangles, where the angles sum to 180°, and quadrilaterals, which can be split into two triangles to give 360°. Explore polygons with more sides by partitioning them into triangles from a single vertex, for example splitting a pentagon into three triangles, making the sum of the interior angles 540°. Encourage students to investigate different polygons and record their findings, noticing how the number of sides links to the number of triangles and the total angle sum. Then introduce regular polygons, showing how each interior angle can be found by dividing the total by the number of sides. Students also identify interior and exterior angles at a vertex and calculate them using their knowledge of angles on a straight line. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that the sum of the interior angles differs between regular and irregular polygons. • Students may assume that the sum of the angles can be found by multiplying the number of sides by 180°. • Students may struggle to split the polygons into triangles, using more than one vertex. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 12 Mathematical talk • How many triangles can a quadrilateral be split into? What does that tell you about the total sum of its interior angles? • If a pentagon can be split into three triangles, what does that tell you about the total sum of its interior angles? • Why is the interior angle sum of any polygon always a multiple of 180°? • Describe the relationship between the number of sides a polygon has and the number of triangles it can be split into from one vertex. • How can you calculate the angle sum of any polygon? Does your method work for concave polygons? National Curriculum links • Derive and use the sum of angles in a triangle and use it to deduce the angle sum in any polygon, and to derive properties of regular polygons E

ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students are introduced to the idea of simple proofs using known angle facts. Distinguish between a demonstration, which shows why something is true in one case, and a proof, which explains why it is always true. Model how the angles in a triangle sum to 180° by cutting out the three corners and rearranging them so that they fit together along a straight line. Encourage students to make links to earlier angle facts, recognising that angles on a straight line sum to 180°. Students should practise writing short proofs, focusing on clear reasoning and step-by-step justification. Discussions about efficiency and generalisation will help students to see how proofs provide certainty and are more powerful than examples alone. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that showing one example is enough to prove a fact. • Students may think that proofs are only shown by calculations, rather than reasoning and logical facts. • Students may write explanations without a clear structure. • Students may struggle with more challenging expressions such as 180 − (90 − x). Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 13 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about a proof and a demonstration? • What do you know? What can you find out? • Is it possible to prove something in more than one way? • How could you prove that there are 360° in a full turn? • Why is it important to write each step of a proof in order? • This trapezium has two right angles. Does this mean that every trapezium has two right angles? Explain how you know. • How can you prove that the angles in a pentagon sum to 540° using the fact that angles in a triangle sum to 180°? National Curriculum links • Apply angle facts, triangle congruence, similarity and properties of quadrilaterals to derive results about angles and sides, including Pythagoras’ theorem, and use known results to obtain simple proofs E

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students investigate the properties of quadrilaterals and their diagonals. A Frayer model can be useful to explore the characteristics of quadrilaterals, as well as providing examples and non-examples. Start by focusing on special quadrilaterals such as squares, rectangles, trapezia, rhombi and parallelograms. Encourage students to consider their similarities as well as how they differ, for example in terms of how many sets of parallel lines or right angles they have. Students can then discuss the fact that diagonals join opposite vertices of a quadrilateral and can sometimes be vertical or horizontal in orientation.

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore the exterior angles of a polygon. Discuss the definition of a polygon, using examples and non-examples to support understanding. Ensure that students are familiar with exterior angles, understanding that they are formed by extending the sides of a polygon and not that they are the remaining angle around the point at each vertex. Establish the relationship between interior and exterior angles, recognising that the two angles will form a straight line and therefore sum to 180°. Then move on to deduce that the exterior angle sum of any polygon is 360°. Ensure that students understand that the exterior angles will only ever be equal when the polygon is regular.
ss_desc: Students examine exterior angles of polygons, understanding they're formed by extending polygon sides, not the remaining vertex angle. small_step_name: Interior angles of a regular polygon
ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore the interior angles of a polygon. Ensure that students are aware that the sum of the interior angle and the exterior angle at a vertex is 180°. Once students are secure in this, move on to calculating the interior angle sum. Use diagrams to explore the relationship between the number of sides a polygon has and the number of internal triangles that can be formed within it. This will lead students to deduce that the interior angle sum is equal to (n − 2 ) × 180°, where n is the number of sides. Challenge students to work out the sizes of unknown angles in a polygon by calculating the interior angle sum.
ss_desc: Students learn about polygon interior angles, understanding that the sum of interior and exterior angles equals 180°. They calculate the interior angle sum, using diagrams to relate polygon sides to internal triangles. This leads to the formula (n-2)×180° for angle sums, and applying it to find unknown angles.

small_step_name: Solve equations with squares and square roots
ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of square numbers and square roots, together with their knowledge of solving equations, to solve equations with square numbers and square roots. Recap calculating square numbers and their square roots. Students apply this knowledge to solve equations that involve squares and square roots, for example x2 = 16 or x = 5. Emphasise the use of inverse operations to solve the equations and highlight why x2 = 16 has two solutions: x = 4 and x = −4. Explain that both 42 = 16 and (−4)2 = 16, so the equation has two values of x that make it true. Therefore, when solving x2 = a, they are looking for all values whose square is a, which includes both the positive and negative values. As students increase in confidence, they move on to solving equations with coefficients that are not 1 and with numbers on both sides of the equation. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not include both positive and negative solutions. • Students may misunderstand the concept of inverse operations with squares and square roots. Explain your answer. • Write a pair of equations, one that has one solution and one that has two. Explain the difference. • Does the equation x2 = a always have two solutions? Explain how you know. small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Pythagoras theorem_2_Identify the hypotenuse

small_step_name: Determine whether a triangle is right-angled
ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students identify the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. Start with several right-angled triangles and ask students to measure the length of each side. Encourage them to identify the side that is opposite the right angle and ask what they notice about its length compared to the other sides. Introduce the term “hypotenuse” and emphasise that this is always the longest side in a right-angled triangle and is always opposite the right angle. Include plenty of examples in different orientations, so that they do not rely on position or direction. Include non-examples to challenge misconceptions. As students develop confidence, ask them to identify the hypotenuses within a compound shape made up of right-angled triangles.
ss_desc: Students learn to identify the hypotenuse in right-angled triangles, understanding it's the longest side and opposite the right angle. They measure triangle sides, observe hypotenuse properties, and apply knowledge to various examples and non-examples. They also identify hypotenuses in compound shapes of right-angled triangles.
small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Pythagoras theorem_3_Determine whether a triangle is right-angled

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore Pythagoras’ theorem and use it to identify right-angled triangles. Start by exploring the areas of the squares on each side of a right-angled triangle. Use concrete or visual representations to support students in discovering that the sum of the areas on the two shorter sides is equal to the area on the side of the hypotenuse. Guide students to notice and articulate this relationship, leading to the formulation of Pythagoras’ theorem, a2 + b2 = c2. Emphasise that the hypotenuse is represented by “c” or “hyp”. Once students understand the connection, ask them to apply the rule to check whether a given triangle is right-angled, using known side lengths to test if the condition is satisfied.
ss_desc: Students explore Pythagoras' theorem, identifying right-angled triangles by comparing square areas on each side. Using visual aids, they discover the sum of areas on the shorter sides equals the hypotenuse's area, formulating a2 + b2 = c2. They apply this rule to verify right-angled triangles using known side lengths.
small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Pythagoras theorem_4_Pythagoras’ theorem (find the hypotenuse)

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate the length of the hypotenuse, given the two shorter sides, building on their knowledge that the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle and that it is the longest side in a right-angled triangle. Start with right-angled triangles in a variety of orientations, encouraging students to identify the hypotenuse before substituting values into the formula a2 + b2 = c2. Emphasise the importance of squaring correctly, adding accurately and remembering to take the square root as the final step. Remind students that answers should often be rounded to a given degree of accuracy, for example 1 decimal place. Encourage students to check whether their answer makes sense by comparing it to the lengths of the other sides. As their confidence develops, introduce problems involving compound shapes, where identifying right-angled triangles is required.
ss_desc: Students calculate the hypotenuse length in right-angled triangles, using the formula a² + b² = c². They identify the hypotenuse, square correctly, add accurately, and take the square root. Answers should be rounded and checked against other side lengths. As confidence grows, they tackle compound shapes with right-angled triangles.
small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Pythagoras theorem_5_Pythagoras’ theorem (find any side)

small_step_name: Use Pythagoras’ theorem on coordinate axes
ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students deepen their understanding of Pythagoras’ theorem by applying it to find the length of any side in a right-angled triangle. Remind students how to identify the hypotenuse and to understand that, when the hypotenuse and one shorter side are known, they need to subtract the square of the shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse before taking the square root. Use diagrams and model the reasoning aloud to support students’ understanding so that they do not simply rely on memorised steps. Once they are confident, introduce questions where the unknown side is sometimes the hypotenuse and sometimes a shorter side. This encourages students to think carefully about which side they are finding and helps to secure a deeper conceptual understanding of the theorem.
ss_desc: Students enhance their grasp of Pythagoras' theorem by determining the length of any side in a right-angled triangle. They learn to identify the hypotenuse, subtract the square of a shorter side from the hypotenuse's square, and take the square root. Varied questions promote careful thought and deeper theorem comprehension.
small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Pythagoras theorem_6_Use Pythagoras’ theorem on coordinate axes

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their knowledge of coordinates by using Pythagoras’ theorem to find the length of a line segment between two points. Start in the first quadrant, drawing a line segment and counting the horizontal and vertical distances to form a right-angled triangle. Use these to apply Pythagoras’ theorem. As confidence grows, sketch coordinates without a grid and ask students how they could calculate the length without counting squares. Encourage clear diagram labelling, accurate subtraction of coordinates and interpreting results in context. Students can then progress to working with all four quadrants and reason about distances without always using a diagram.
ss_desc: Students enhance coordinate knowledge by applying Pythagoras' theorem to determine line segment lengths between two points. Starting in the first quadrant, they form a right-angled triangle, then calculate lengths without grid reliance. Emphasize diagram labelling, coordinate subtraction, and context interpretation. Progress to all quadrants and reasoning distances without diagrams.
small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Pythagoras theorem_7_Proofs of Pythagoras’ theorem E

ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students explore a range of proofs for Pythagoras’ theorem. Algebraic and geometric proofs are examples of proofs that can be explored. It is useful to begin by using a visual or dynamic demonstration to make the result feel intuitive, before introducing a more formal algebraic or geometric proof. Perigal’s dissection was introduced in Step 3, when students were using the theorem to determine whether a triangle is right-angled, and it may be beneficial to refer back to this to support understanding. This step is an opportunity to revisit the proof in a richer context and highlight that Pythagoras’ theorem is not just a formula to memorise, but a result with multiple clear and convincing justifications.
ss_desc: In this step, students examine various proofs of Pythagoras' theorem, including algebraic and geometric ones. The use of visual aids, such as Perigal's dissection, aids comprehension. This stage emphasizes that Pythagoras' theorem is more than a memorized formula, offering multiple convincing justifications.

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore independent events. It can be helpful to introduce the idea through a sample space diagram, for example for rolling two dice, where all possible outcomes can be listed and favourable cases counted. Draw students’ attention to how this method produces the same result as multiplying the separate probabilities, for example 1 2 × 1 6 = 1 12 for rolling an even number on one dice and a 5 on the other. ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students describe a translation using a column vector. Encourage students to identify a pair of corresponding vertices, then model how to calculate the horizontal and vertical movements needed to map one onto the other. ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning of angles in triangles and quadrilaterals from Key Stage 3. Begin with the fact that the angles in a triangle sum to 180°, then use this to divide a quadrilateral into two triangles, showing that the angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Use a variety of different types of triangles and quadrilaterals and discuss the similar vocabulary around these, such as “isosceles triangle” and “isosceles trapezium”. Discuss what these terms inform us about the angles. Encourage students to explain their answers and to label angles accurately using three-letter notation. ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their prior learning of interior and exterior angles from Key Stage 3. Remind them that the sum of the exterior angles of any polygon is 360° and use this to calculate individual exterior angles in regular polygons by dividing 360° by the number of sides. Highlight that interior and exterior angles sum to 180°, and use this to calculate unknown exterior angles given an interior angle. Students can then extend this knowledge to find the number of sides of a regular polygon when either the interior or exterior angle is known. Encourage students to clearly label diagrams to support reasoning, and to help identify when sides or angles are equal. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that the exterior and interior angles sum to 360°. • Students may believe that the sum of exterior angles depends on the number of sides the polygon has. • Students may assume that some equal angles always mean the polygon is regular, without checking that all sides are also equal in length. ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning of interior angles of polygons from Key Stage 3. Begin by revisiting the relationship between interior and exterior angles. Highlight that they form a straight line and therefore sum to 180°. Remind students that the sum of interior angles can be calculated using (n – 2) × 180°, where n is the number of sides, and that this can also be used to work out the number of sides when the sum of interior angles is known. It can be useful to model splitting polygons into triangles to demonstrate why this method works to calculate the sum of interior angles. Reinforce that “regular” means that all sides and angles are equal. Calculators may be used throughout this step, so the focus remains on the method rather than the arithmetic. ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students begin to use clear reasoning to prove geometric facts. Start by revisiting familiar angle facts, ensuring students can state each fact accurately. ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning from Year 8 on drawing and interpreting pie charts. Remind students that a pie chart represents a whole split into parts, with each sector showing a fraction of the total and all sectors summing to 360°. Make clear links between proportions, fractions and angles to show how they describe the same information. Emphasise the accurate use of a protractor when constructing sectors and highlight the importance of clear labelling. Introduce data given as percentages, fractions or bar charts for conversion into a pie chart. ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their Year 7 learning on drawing and interpreting time series graphs. Remind them that these graphs show changes over time and require clearly labelled axes for accurate interpretation. Emphasise that time is always plotted on the horizontal axis and that equal intervals are essential. Encourage students to discuss upward or downward trends, along with periods of stability. ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret frequency polygons. Begin by modelling how to construct a frequency polygon by identifying the midpoint of each class interval, plotting these points and joining them with straight lines. Highlight that the horizontal axis shows data from the class intervals as a continuous scale and the vertical axis shows the frequencies. Discuss with students why midpoints of the class intervals are used to plot the data on the horizontal axis and to describe what the shape of the frequency polygon shows, such as increases or decreases in the data. Model how to compare two frequency polygons on the same axes and explain how the overall shape helps students interpret and compare different distributions. ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret stem-and-leaf diagrams. Begin by explaining that these diagrams organise numerical data, using the stem to show place value and the leaf to show the final digit, allowing all values to remain visible. Emphasise that including a clear key is essential so the data can be correctly interpreted. Model how to organise the data, select a suitable stem, and record each leaf clearly so digits align. Revisit how to calculate averages and the range by finding the difference between the greatest and smallest values in the set. Recap that histograms show continuous data and that the area of each bar represents frequency. Guide students to examine a single bar and identify what they know, such as the class boundaries and the height. Ask students how these two features could be used to calculate the frequency. Support students to derive the relationship, frequency = frequency density × class width. Provide opportunities to estimate values within an interval, including estimating a value for the median by accumulating frequencies. Encourage students to express parts of the distribution as fractions and percentages once they have calculated the total frequency. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe the frequency is represented by the height of the bar rather than the area. • Students may use class midpoints rather than class boundaries when estimating values. Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Graphs and diagrams_7_Frequency polygons

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore how cumulative frequency diagrams are constructed from grouped data. Begin by discussing how the total builds as we add on the frequency from each class interval and guide students to recognise that cumulative frequency represents a running total. Highlight that these totals are plotted at the upper boundary of the class interval. Ask students to discuss the shape of the diagram, noticing that it can rise or stay level but never fall. Highlight that a cumulative frequency diagram can be plotted with either a smooth curve or straight line segments. It can be helpful to demonstrate the plotting process under a visualiser so students can watch each step clearly as the cumulative frequency diagram is formed. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may plot cumulative frequencies at the midpoint of class boundaries instead of the upper boundaries. • Students may plot frequencies from a given table rather than a cumulative frequency. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 7 Mathematical talk • What does the cumulative frequency tell us about the data up to a given point? • How does adding each class frequency change the cumulative total? • Are cumulative frequency diagrams always plotted at the upper boundary? Explain your answer. • Can the shape of a cumulative frequency diagram show a decrease? Why or why not? • How are the plotted points joined? • What is the same and what is different between a frequency polygon and a cumulative frequency diagram? H National Curriculum links • {construct and interpret diagrams for grouped discrete data and continuous data, i.e. histograms with equal and unequal class intervals and cumulative frequency graphs and know their appropriate use}

Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Graphs and diagrams_8_Stem-and-leaf diagrams

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of cumulative frequency diagrams by interpreting the data shown. Remind students that each plotted point represents a cumulative total. Guide students to identify an estimate for the median and lower and upper quartiles by finding 25%, 50% and 75% of the total frequency and locating these values on the curve. Students then calculate the interquartile range by subtracting the lower quartile from the upper quartile. They should also be able to compare two cumulative frequency diagrams by considering the median and interquartile range and deduce what these comparisons indicate. Encourage accurate reading of values by drawing horizontal and vertical lines and discuss why this method is more reliable than estimating by eye. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may attempt to find quartiles using the horizontal axis instead of the cumulative frequency axis. • Students may read values directly from the curve without drawing horizontal and vertical lines, resulting in inaccuracies. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 8 Mathematical talk • What does each plotted point represent on a cumulative frequency diagram? • How do we know where to find 25%, 50% and 75% of the data? • Why are the values for the median, upper and lower quartiles only an estimate? • What does the interquartile range tell us about the distribution of the data? • What does the graph tell us about the value below which 10% of the data lies? • Why can’t the range be identified from a grouped frequency table or a cumulative frequency table? H National Curriculum links • {construct and interpret diagrams for grouped discrete data and continuous data, i.e. histograms with equal and unequal class intervals and cumulative frequency graphs and know their appropriate use} • interpret, analyse and compare the distributions of data sets from univariate empirical distributions through: appropriate measures of central tendency (including modal class) and spread {including quartiles and inter-quartile range}
small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_8_Interpret cumulative frequency diagrams

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn how to represent the distribution of data sets by drawing box plots. Highlight that a box plot is formed from 5 values from a given data set: the median, the upper and lower quartiles and the minimum and maximum values. Use of a visualiser is recommended when modelling how to draw a box plot. Students can also explore the relationships between data represented on a cumulative frequency diagram and a box plot and identify quartiles carefully before drawing a box plot. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misinterpret scales when drawing box plots. • Students may not recognise that they need to calculate missing values needed to draw a box plot. For example, if they are given the range and the lowest value, they need to work out the maximum value. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 9 Mathematical talk • What five key values do we need to know to draw a box plot? • Which line segment represents the median? • What does the length of the box represent? • How does the box plot show the spread that we see on the cumulative frequency graph? • How can we use a cumulative frequency graph to find the median and the upper and lower quartiles? • Why is it important to read values accurately from the scale? • How can we check that our box plot matches the information from the cumulative frequency graph? • How can we calculate the interquartile range from the box plot? H National Curriculum links • Interpret, analyse and compare the distributions of data sets from univariate empirical distributions through: appropriate graphical representation involving discrete, continuous and grouped data, {including box plots}
small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_9_Box plots

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn how to compare distributions using box plots. Remind students that a box plot summarises a data set using the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum values, allowing two or more distributions to be compared quickly on the same scale. Emphasise that comparisons should focus on a measure of average (median) and spread (range or interquartile range). Highlight that the relative positions of the medians can be used to decide which data set has the higher typical value. Encourage students to compare lengths of the boxes to judge differences in the interquartile ranges and discuss which data set shows greater consistency. Highlight the importance of using the same continuous scale so that comparisons are valid. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may draw incorrect conclusions, for example interpreting a larger range as an average or vice versa. • Students may incorrectly interpret the interquartile range or range, for example thinking a larger interquartile range is ‘better’. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 10 Mathematical talk • How do the positions of the medians help you compare trends in data sets? • Why is analysing the medians alone not enough to compare two data sets? • Which distribution shows a greater spread of data? How do you know? • How do the interquartile ranges compare? • What does a smaller interquartile range reveal about the spread of the middle half of the data? • How can you tell which data set is more consistent? • What do the “whiskers” tell you about the extremes in each data set? • What is the difference between the range and the interquartile range? Which of these measures might be affected by an outlier? Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Vectors_1_Understand and represent vectors

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of vectors beyond the context of translating shapes, which they previously encountered in Year 9. This step will focus on interpreting column vectors and representing vectors as diagrams. Remind students that the top number in a column vector represents the horizontal direction, while the bottom number represents the vertical direction. It is important that students understand that a vector shows both direction and magnitude. The role of the arrow should also be emphasised, as it indicates the start point, end point, and direction of the vector. Comparing similar vectors can help to reinforce this understanding, for example by comparing 3 4 -   and -3 4   . Misconceptions and common errors • Students may neglect to draw arrows on vectors. • Students may draw arrows in the wrong direction on vectors. • Students may misinterpret column vectors, such as reading 2 4 -   as ‘2 up and 4 left’ rather than ‘2 right and 4 down’. Explain how you know. • How do you know which direction to draw the arrow? • What is the same and what is different about the vectors -2 5   and 2 5 -   ? • Is it possible to draw a vector without an arrow? Explain your answer. Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Vectors_2_Vector notation

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of vector representations as column vectors and directed line segments by introducing notation for labelling vectors. Different conventions should be introduced, such as writing a vector as AB , emphasising that this represents the vector from A to B. Comparing related vectors can further deepen understanding of vectors as movements between points, for example by comparing AB with BA . Students should also be given opportunities to work with vectors labelled using bold letters, such as a or x. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misinterpret vectors, for example reading XY as YX . • Students may neglect to draw arrows on the vectors or draw arrows in the wrong direction. • Students may neglect to label vectors. For example, not labelling ‘E’ and ‘F’ on either end of a line segment to represent the vector EF . Year 10 | Summer term | Block 3 – Vectors | Step 2 Mathematical talk • What is the significance of the order of the letters in the vector AB ? How does this differ from the vector BA ? • Do the letters describing a vector always have to be in alphabetical order? Explain how you know. • If vector a = 3 4   what would –a represent? Explain how you know. • How can two vectors have the same magnitude but different directions? Write an example. • If CD = 2 3  , how would you represent CD on a grid? • If CD = 2 3  , how would you represent DC on a grid? Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Vectors_3_Translate by a vector

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore vectors that are parallel to each other. Introduce students to the concept of a scalar, emphasising that it is the value by which a vector is multiplied. Students should recognise that when one vector is a scalar multiple of another, the two vectors are parallel. Begin by using diagrams to represent different vectors, for example by comparing a and 2a on a grid, highlighting that both are parallel and that 2a is twice the magnitude of a. This can then be used to build towards multiplying column vectors by a scalar. Emphasise that both the horizontal and vertical components of a column vector are multiplied by the scalar. Students should also have opportunities to explore the effect of multiplying vectors by negative scalars; for example, multiplying by –1 reverses the direction of a vector. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly when calculating with negative numbers. • Students may neglect to multiply both values in a column vector by the scalar. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 3 – Vectors | Step 3 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about parallel vectors? • Can two vectors be parallel but not equal in magnitude? Explain how you know. • How do we know if one vector is a multiple of the other? • What is a scalar? • What is the effect of multiplying a vector by a negative scalar? • How does multiplying a vector by a scalar change its magnitude? Does it ever change its direction? H National Curriculum links • Describe translations as 2D vectors • Apply addition and subtraction of vectors, multiplication of vectors by a scalar, and diagrammatic and column representations of vectors; {use vectors to construct geometric arguments and proofs}

Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Vectors_4_Vectors multiplied by a scalar

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn how to add column vectors. Remind students that a vector has a horizontal component and a vertical component and that these components can be represented as column vectors. Emphasise that when adding two vectors, the resultant vector is found by adding the horizontal components together and the vertical components together. As with previous steps, visual representations of addition of vectors can help students to build a deeper understanding. Provide opportunities to draw vector diagrams to show how one vector follows another, making the connection between the geometric path and the numerical calculation. Once learning is secure move on to more abstract calculations, such as adding two column vectors. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly when using negative numbers. • Students may draw vectors incorrectly, such as drawing arrows facing the wrong direction. Explain your reasoning. • Why do we add the horizontal components and add the vertical components to find the resultant vector? • What happens if we add vector a to vector –a? Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Vectors_5_Add vectors

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students deepen their understanding of arithmetic with vectors by learning how to subtract vectors. As with previous steps, representing vector subtraction using diagrams is a helpful approach before introducing formal written methods. This can be introduced by considering equivalent calculations, such as a – b and a + (–b). Once students are confident, they can practise adding and subtracting vectors abstractly. If appropriate, challenge students to solve problems that combine operations such as multiplication with addition or subtraction, for example, 2 × 3 4   + 2 5 -  . Misconceptions and common errors • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly when using negative numbers. • Students may struggle to represent vector subtraction problems as diagrams. • Students may neglect one of the values in a column vector when multiplying by a scalar. For example, writing –1 × 3 5 -   = - - 3 5  . Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Vectors_6_Add and subtract vectors

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore different ways to express vector journeys, combining successive movements as vector calculations. This step builds the foundations needed for students to form geometric proofs later. Students learn to express a route such as AB + BC + CD = AD showing that multiple vectors can represent a single resultant vector. Students then move to simplifying expressions or comparing routes algebraically, for example, by writing a + b + 2a – b as 3a. Draw students’ attention to the fact that different routes can have the same resultant vector. Highlight the effect of reversing the direction of a vector, for example, if MN = a – 2b then NM = –a + 2b. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may neglect the direction of arrows on a vector diagram, such as using the vector a rather than –a. • Students may struggle to find a route using known vectors. • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly with negative terms. Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Vectors_7_Solve problems with vectors (E)

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students apply their knowledge of vector journeys while considering the properties of quadrilaterals such as rectangles, parallelograms, and trapezia. Encourage students to discuss the properties of different quadrilaterals, for example, parallelograms have two pairs of parallel sides. Highlight that this means a parallelogram has two pairs of identical vectors. Draw students’ attention to the direction of arrows on diagrams and how this can affect the result of a vector journey and the accurate evaluation of vector addition or subtraction. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may neglect the direction of arrows on a vector diagram, such as using the vector a rather than –a. • Students may not recognise properties leading to vectors which aren’t labelled on diagrams. For example, using the fact that opposite sides in a parallelogram are parallel and equal in length. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 3 – Vectors | Step 7 Mathematical talk • Which quadrilaterals have pairs of parallel sides? How many pairs of parallel vectors will they have? • ‘A square has four equal vectors.’ Explain why the statement is false. • How can we describe each side of the quadrilateral using vectors? • What does it mean if two sides have equal vectors? • What does the direction of the arrow tell us about a vector? • If AB = a – 2b what is BA in terms of a and b? • How can we use vector relationships to identify the type of quadrilateral? ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore parallel vectors, recognising that vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other. Students may have some understanding of this concept from earlier steps in this block. Highlight that parallel vectors have the same (or opposite) direction but may differ in magnitude. Support strategies for proving that column vectors are parallel by using vectors represented on grids to emphasise the link between vectors and scalars. After this, model how to prove that algebraic vectors are parallel through factorisation. Once students are confident, move on to more complex problems where they may need to consider vector journeys to compare two vectors. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think vectors are parallel if they have the same magnitude. • Students may not recognise parallel vectors involving negative scalars. For example, writing 6 2 -   as –2 × -3 1   to show 6 2 -   and -3 1   are parallel. • Students may find it difficult to write algebraic expressions for vectors that represent movement in the opposite direction. Explain how you know. • How can we tell if two vectors in terms of a and b are parallel? • What happens to a vector when it is multiplied by a negative scalar? • Why do parallel vectors not have to be equal in length? • Are two vectors that are equal in magnitude always parallel? Why or why not? Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Factors and powers_1_Factors, multiples and primes

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap finding the highest common factor (HCF), lowest common multiple (LCM), and writing numbers as a product of prime factors from Key Stage 3. Use practical contexts to reinforce when HCF or LCM is needed, and model listing with small numbers to show why it becomes inefficient for greater values. Revisit prime factorisation using factor trees, emphasising that every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation. Use Venn diagrams to organise information, highlighting that the HCF is the product of the common factors, while the LCM is the product of all factors within the diagram. Link back to listing to show both methods give the same result. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may include non-prime factors in their final product. • Students may confuse factors and multiples, particularly when using listing methods. • Students may rely on listing methods for large numbers, leading to inefficiency and increased likelihood of error. • Students may multiply all prime factors when finding the HCF, rather than only those common to all numbers. Why or why not? • Is there more than one way to express 84 as a product of prime factors? • Does the order of the factors in a prime factorisation matter? Explain your answer. • What is the same and what is different between 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 23 × 3? • How do you find the HCF using a Venn diagram? • How do you find the LCM using a Venn diagram? Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Factors and powers_2_Prime factorisation

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap evaluating powers and roots, both mentally and using a calculator. Reinforce that a root is the inverse of a power, and ensure students can use calculator functions for powers and roots greater than 3. Support estimation by identifying the two integers a root lies between. Emphasise that a negative index does not make the value negative but instead indicates a reciprocal. Demonstrate this using a decreasing pattern, for example 22 = 4, 21 = 2, 20 = 1 and 2–1 = 1 2. Encourage students to generalise this to show that for any non-zero value of a, a–n = 1 an . Model converting negative indices into fractions with positive indices using numerical and algebraic examples, extending to bases with coefficients as confidence develops. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may assume that a negative index results in a negative answer, for example 3–2 = –9 • Students may multiply the base by the index instead of using a reciprocal, for example 2–3 = –6 • Students may misuse calculator functions for powers and roots, leading to incorrect evaluations. Explain your answer. • What is the same and what is different about 64 and 64 6 ? • If 54 = 625, what is the 4th root of 625? How do you know? • What is the same and what is different between 3–2 and 1 32 ? • Which is greater: 2–3 or 2–5? Explain your answer • If a–2 = 1 25 , what is the value of a? Explain how you know. • How else can you write a–4? • Explain why the value of a in a–1 cannot be equal to zero. H National Curriculum links • Use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube and higher), recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, 5 and distinguish between exact representations of roots and their decimal approximations (KS3)

Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Factors and powers_3_HCF and LCM

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore fractional indices. Some students may have previously covered this as an extend step in Year 8. Ensure students are fluent with square roots, cube roots and higher roots before introducing fractional indices using numerical bases. Develop understanding by reasoning from index laws, for example 9 1 2 × 9 1 2 = 91, and link this to 9 = 3 since 3 × 3 = 9. Use this to generalise that the denominator of a fractional index indicates the root. Once students are confident with unit fractional indices, introduce non-unit fractional indices, emphasising that the numerator represents a power applied after the root. Extend to fractional bases and negative fractional indices by linking back to negative indices as reciprocals. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the roles of the numerator and denominator, for example interpreting 64 3 2 as a cube root squared instead of a square root cubed. • Students may attempt to calculate a fraction of the base rather than taking the root and then applying the power. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 3 Mathematical talk • Explain why a 1 2 × a 1 2 = a1 • If 4 1 2 × 4 1 2 = 41, what is the value of 4 1 2 ? • What operation is a fractional power equivalent to? • What root is a power of a half/third equivalent to? Explain how you know. • How else can x 1 4 be written? • How can you generalise a rule for fractional indices? • If you know the value of x 1 3 , how can you find the value of – x 1 3? • What is the same and what is different about calculating 2 –3 64 and 3 –2 64 ? H National Curriculum links • Calculate with roots, and with integer {and fractional} indices

Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Factors and powers_4_Square and cube numbers

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students work with all four operations involving surds. The focus is on adding/subtracting like surds and multiplying/dividing surds by surds/integers. At this stage, surds do not need to be simplified beyond an integer result. For example, 3 × 5 can remain as 15, while 4 × 4 simplifies to 4. This keeps the focus on structure rather than technique, with further surd simplification developed in the next step. When adding and subtracting, emphasise that only like surds can be combined, just as only like algebraic terms can be collected, for example, 3 2 + 5 2 = 8 2 but 2 + 3 cannot be simplified further. When multiplying, model that a × b æ ab and that multiplying by an integer scales the surd, for example a × b = a b. If students are secure, you may choose to combine this step with simplifying surds further. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may try to add or subtract surds with different bases, for example 2 + 3 • Students may multiply integers and surds incorrectly, for example writing 2 × 5 = 10 • Students may not recognise when the product of surds simplifies to an integer, such as 4 × 4 = 4 Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 4 Mathematical talk • Are surds rational or irrational? • When we multiply/divide two surds, what happens to the numbers inside the square roots? • Explain why 4 × 4 is equivalent to 4 • Is a + a equivalent to 2a ? Why or why not? • Why does 2 × 3 not give an integer answer? • What stays the same and what changes when we multiply a surd by an integer? • Why can we not add surds with different bases, for example 2 + 3? • How is adding and subtracting surds similar to working with algebraic terms? H National Curriculum links • Simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions (including those involving surds) {and algebraic fractions} by: factorising quadratic expressions of the form x2 + bx + c, including the difference of two squares; {factorising quadratic expressions of the form ax2 + bx + c}; simplifying expressions involving sums, products and powers, including the laws of indices
small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_4_Four operations with surds
Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Factors and powers_5_Powers and roots

ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of surds by exploring how the number inside a square root affects how it can be simplified. Model how to simplify surds by rewriting the number inside the root as a product including a square factor, for example 18 = 9 × 2. Emphasise the importance of identifying a square factor as the result of square rooting a square number will be an integer. Highlight that it is often efficient to identify the greatest square factor to simplify a surd. If students cannot spot a square factor encourage the use of a factor tree to show the prime factorisation, for example 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 . Emphasise that this method relies on pairing equal factors to form a square number that can be square rooted. Once students are confident, extend this to other contexts such as area calculations or simplifying algebraic expressions. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not fully simplify a surd, leaving a square factor inside the square root when more than one square factor is present. ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students rationalise denominators that contain a single surd, building on their understanding of surds and rational numbers.
